Which solo adventure's to unlock first?

So the two of them both have useful cards, but I think that Naxx is definitely the better one to get first.

From Naxx the useful cards that you get are:

Nerubian Egg: Zoo, shaman, etc.

Unstable Ghoul: Patron warrior, you would need BRM for the patron though

Sludge Belcher: Solid midrange card in many decks

Deathlord: arguable viability, only in priest

Mad Scientist: Every hunter and mage deck

Zombie chow: Many, many decks

Shade of Naxx: Midrange druid and some random OTK priests

Loatheb: Many decks

Kel'thuzad: Arguable viability, ramp druid and reincarnate shaman

Duplicate: Echo and some tempo/control mages

Webspinner: Basically every hunter deck

Voidcaller: Demonlock

Death's bite: Every warrior deck except maybe some face decks

Dark Cultist: Old control priest lists, less used now but still very strong overally

From Blackrock Mountain the useful cards you get are:

Grim Patron: Patron warrior, obviously

Druid of the Flame: Arguable viability, I've seen it in Midrange druid but not often

Imp Gang Boss: Demonlock and Zoo

Flamewaker: Aggro mage, tempo mage

Fireguard destroyer: Arguable viability, it would be great in basically every shaman deck but nobody is playing shaman so it's hard to say

Quickshot: Most hunter decks

Emperor Thaurissan: Many combo decks: Freeze mage, oil rogue, etc.

Nefarian: Control decks, arguable Ysera replacement

Another note, all the rest of the dragon cards are okay and they show up in things like the chinese dragon control warrior and people have tried to make dragon decks but none of them are really great except the warrior.

Wow thats a really useful list, thanks a bunch!

I have a quick question on one of the cards.

"Zombie chow: Many, many decks" - Is this card actually any good? I am a bit put off by the healing.

Zombie Chow is absolutely excellent. But it's one card that takes a little bit to understand the purpose of it. In aggro decks where the opponents HP dropping and staying low, it's fairly useless. It excels against aggro decks.

For example, look at a Ramp Druid vs a Face Hunter opener. The Face Hunter's opening hand holds leper gnome and webspinner. They open with either of those, and you play the Zombie chow. It will 2 for 1 vs these two cards, protect your HP and end up "healing" the hunter for a total of zero since they will not have taken damage yet. Later in the game, it can absolutely be a dead draw because of the healing but early game vs aggro it is a game changer.

Edit: As well, it trades for 3/2's like Acidic Swamp Ooze and Sorcerer's Apprentice.

The movie "Event Horizon" has elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, or possibly takes place in the distant past of the Warhammer 40k universe.

In the Cthulhu Mythos[1] version, the Event Horizon while testing an experimental warp drive encounters beings humans couldn't possibly understand. This causes the first crew to go insane and kill each other/themselves. Sam Neil's character (already emotionally unstable by the death of his wife) then also goes insane when he realizes the horrible truth about what happened to the first crew. He then attempts to return the ship to the warp, bringing more sacrifices to those incomprehensible beings.

In a the Warhammer 40K universe, warp travel requires passing through the Immaterium to traverse the vast distances of interstellar space. Ships have to be shielded from malevolent beings while in the warp or risk being ravaged. The first crew of the Event Horizon while testing an experimental warp drive in an unshielded vessel die horribly when they encounter these warp beings. When the ship finally returns to our solar system, its still "haunted" by warp entities that then latch onto Sam Neil’s character (he is mentally weakened by the death of his wife) and attempt to use him to bring fresh victims into the warp.
The movie Event Horizon takes place in either the Cthulhu Mythos or perhaps a pre Warhammer 40k universe

That's fascinating, thanks for sharing! Event Horizon is a personal favorite of mine...my friends and I probably went and saw it nearly a dozen times. I'm familiar with Cthulhu but thanks for making me aware of Warhammer as well :)

It is a compelling idea (one which has been discussed on that other website).

The 40k timeline has been well established. The current date is 015.M3 (2015) per the Imperial Date System, while the current time in universe is 935.M41 (40,935). The various collected works places humanity's development of warp travel in M18 and subsequently heralds in the 'Dark Age of Technology' when humankind reached the pinnacle of their technological prowess and experienced explosive growth into the galaxy. Prior to M18, humanity began expanding using sub-light travel in M15, necessitating the use of generational ships, cyrogenic sleep, seed ships, and other conventional modes of transportation. This period ends in M22 with the appearance of psykers and the subsequent birth of Slannesh that marked the fall of the Eldar race. Due to this event (the Age of Strife), warp storms prevented warp travel until M30 when the warp storms abated, allowing the Emperor to embark on the Great Crusade, forging the Imperium, and leading up to the current events of M41.

While the aesthetic of the Event Horizon is very reminiscent of Imperial designs, the film concretely places its events squarely within M3, 15000 years before the invention of both the Warp Drive and the Geller Field which is necessary for warp travel. Sadly this makes it linking Event Horizon to 40k a stretch of the imagination, both within the relative time frames it would take to develop the technology and in the ship design itself, as no data exists within the currently established cannon to describe pre-Imperial ship design and aesthetics. It would be highly unlikely that human ship design would maintain its consistency between the two Era's given the derivative nature of Imperial technology and the necessity of it having to be rediscovered after the Age of Strife.

As for the Mythos stuff, EH really fits the thematic backbone of unknowable cosmic horror and the subsequent insanity that a greater understanding of the universe brings with it.

It's much easier to place dated events in the future of a series which doesn't establish any future events in time than it is to fit them in into the opposite.
